displayQuote: Watch the costs and the profits take care of themselves

meta.title: Who really said "Watch the costs and the profits take care of themselves"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Andrew Carnegie, but no book, speech or letter of his contains it. The documented printings are a 1913 trade journal and a 1921 advertisement.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Watch the costs and the profits take care of themselves'?
meta.ogDescription: No Carnegie source has been found for this motto. The near-exact wordings printed between 1913 and 1923 are anonymous American trade-press lines — one of them an ad.

answer.label: Not Andrew Carnegie’s wording — an unsourced motto
answer.sourceLine: The idea is unmistakably Carnegie’s — he built Carnegie Steel on knowing the cost of every process, and said so in his own memoir — but the sentence is not. It appears in neither his Autobiography nor The Empire of Business, Wikiquote files it under “Undated” with nothing behind it but a link to a PBS documentary page, and the earliest printings anyone has documented are anonymous American trade-journal wordings from 1913 and an engineering firm’s advertisement from 1921.

source.heading: What the record actually holds

docMeta.dd: No source has been found in any Carnegie book, speech, letter or interview
American trade journals, a corporate booklet and an advertisement, 1911–1923 (chronology by Barry Popik)
Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920), chap. 10, “The Iron Works”
PBS American Experience → Wikiquote (“Undated”) → quotation sites

source.excerpt: As I became acquainted with the manufacture of iron I was greatly surprised to find that the cost of each of the various processes was unknown. … I felt as if we were moles burrowing in the dark, and this to me was intolerable. I insisted upon such a system of weighing and accounting being introduced throughout our works as would enable us to know what our cost was for each process and especially what each man was doing, who saved material, who wasted it, and who produced the best results.
trail: Wikiquote files the line in its Undated ↗ section, and the only citation beneath it is a bare link to a PBS page — the standard signature of a quotation for which no document has ever been produced.

That bare link points at the American Experience film-transcript page — a legacy URL that is now dead and redirects to the programme’s homepage. The same motto appears, equally uncited, on the American Experience biography of Carnegie ↗, which says he “managed by the motto ‘watch costs, and the profits take care of themselves’” — a documentary’s summary sentence, with no source given for the motto.

Barry Popik’s dated citations ↗ find the wording in the trade press rather than in Carnegie: Domestic Engineering for 17 May 1913 (“Take care of the costs and the profits will take care of themselves”), and all but the exact wording as an L. V. Estes, Incorporated advertisement in Industrial Management for 1 June 1921, whose display type reads “Watch the Costs the Profits Take Care of Themselves” — no “and” — repeated in that form in Management Engineering for 1922–1923.

Carnegie’s own volumes come up empty. Neither the Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie ↗ (1920) nor The Empire of Business ↗ (1902), his collection of business advice, contains “watch the costs” or “take care of themselves” anywhere in its text.
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote. It is the closest documented thing Carnegie actually wrote on the subject — from chapter 10 of his posthumous Autobiography — and it is offered here to show what the record does contain, and what it does not.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the quotation, because no one has identified the work it first appeared in. The passage excerpted above is a different matter: the Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie was published in 1920 and is in the public domain in the United States, which is why Project Gutenberg carries it in full.

author.name: Andrew Carnegie
author.kicker: The man it is pinned on
author.heading: About Andrew Carnegie
author.bio: Carnegie emigrated from Dunfermline as a boy, rose through the telegraph office and the Pennsylvania Railroad, and turned Pittsburgh iron and steel into the largest such enterprise in the world before selling out in 1901 and giving the proceeds away. What made the mills formidable was not invention but measurement: he forced a weighing-and-accounting system on works whose owners, by his own account, did not know what any single process cost. That obsession is documented in his own words — which is precisely why a slogan he never wrote sticks to him so easily.

misattribution.heading: The attribution, taken apart
misattribution.intro: This is a slogan in search of a speaker. Every step of its chain of custody points at a documentary blurb rather than a document.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it under Undated ↗ — quotes it cannot tie to a dated work — and the citation attached is a bare link to a PBS documentary page, not to anything Carnegie wrote or said.

items.who: PBS American Experience (and the quote sites downstream of it)
items.why: The American Experience biography ↗ states that Carnegie “managed by the motto ‘watch costs, and the profits take care of themselves’” and gives no source; the quotation sites repeat it with a tidier wording and quotation marks.

items.who: The American trade press, and an engineering firm’s copywriter
items.why: Barry Popik’s chronology ↗ has Domestic Engineering printing “Take care of the costs and the profits will take care of themselves” on 17 May 1913 as its own maxim, and all but the exact wording — “Watch the Costs the Profits Take Care of Themselves,” without the “and” — running as display type in an advertisement for L. V. Estes, Incorporated, industrial engineers, in Industrial Management on 1 June 1921. Neither mentions Carnegie, and the 1921 advertisement appeared after his death in August 1919.

The pattern is the pence-and-pounds proverb rebuilt for managers. Carnegie quotes the original in An American Four-in-Hand in Britain ↗ — “Take care of your pence and the pounds will take care of themselves” — crediting it there to Franklin.

misattribution.truthLine: The substance is genuinely his: in chapter 10 of his Autobiography ↗ Carnegie describes an iron trade that did not know its own costs and says he felt “as if we were moles burrowing in the dark” until he imposed a system of weighing and accounting. The slogan is a fair summary of that conviction — it simply is not a sentence anyone can show he uttered.

context.heading: Why it sticks to him anyway
lead: Carnegie really did run on costs. In chapter 10 of his Autobiography he describes discovering that the Pittsburgh iron trade had no idea what any of its processes cost — owners learned whether they had made money only when the books were balanced at year’s end — and says he found it intolerable, “as if we were moles burrowing in the dark.” He forced scales and clerks into the works until he knew the cost of every process and the output of every man. A one-line slogan compresses that whole programme neatly, which is most of why it travels under his name.

The phrasing also rides an older rhythm. “Take care of the pence and the pounds will take care of themselves” was a stock English proverb, and Carnegie printed a version of it himself in An American Four-in-Hand in Britain ↗, where his mother offers “Take care of your pence and the pounds will take care of themselves” as one of Franklin’s wisest proverbs. Swap pence for costs and pounds for profits and you have the management version — which is roughly what the American trade press did in the 1910s and 1920s, without crediting anybody.
context.detailsSummary: What the dated citations actually show
detailsBody: Barry Popik’s chronology runs from 1911 to 1923 and never lands on Carnegie. A 1911 Burroughs Adding Machine booklet has “profits will take care of themselves when he has taken care of the losses”; Domestic Engineering ran the near-exact form on 17 May 1913; The Business of Trading in Stocks (1917) applies it to losses rather than costs.

The closest wording to the one quoted today appears in his chronology as display type in an advertisement — “Watch the Costs the Profits Take Care of Themselves,” without the “and”: Industrial Management, 1 June 1921, page 19, for L. V. Estes, Incorporated, industrial engineers — printed after Carnegie’s death in August 1919 — and again in Management Engineering for 1922–1923. Popik marks the entry “in progress,” so earlier printings may yet turn up; what has not turned up is a Carnegie source.

schema.verdictNote: Universally credited to Andrew Carnegie, but no source for the sentence has been found in his books, speeches or letters, and Wikiquote files it as undated with nothing behind it but a bare link to a PBS documentary page. The earliest documented printings are anonymous American trade-press lines of 1913–1923 — one of them an advertisement published after his death — and the true author is not established.

V. Estes, Incorporated advertisement in Industrial Management, 1 June 1921, p. 19; Management Engineering vol. 1, 1922-1923, p. Wikiquote's Andrew Carnegie page carries 'Watch the costs and the profits take care of themselves.' under the section heading 'Undated', with a bare PBS link as its only citation.

PBS American Experience's Carnegie biography states: 'Carnegie was ruthless in keeping down costs and managed by the motto "watch costs, and the profits take care of themselves."' and gives no citation for it.

The full text of the Autobiography of Andrew Carnegie (1920, ed. John C. Van Dyke, London: Constable & Co.) contains the chapter 10 'The Iron Works' passage quoted here ('...the cost of each of the various processes was unknown... I felt as if we were moles burrowing in the dark...'), and contains neither 'watch the costs' nor 'take care of themselves' anywhere in the book.
The full text of Carnegie's The Empire of Business (1902) contains neither 'watch the costs'/'watch costs' nor 'take care of themselves'.
Carnegie's An American Four-in-Hand in Britain prints the proverb 'Take care of your pence and the pounds will take care of themselves,' spoken by his mother and credited there to Benjamin Franklin.
